entities.name: Currently available AI systems increase an actor's biological-misuse capability
entities.note: Candidate proposition for this pack. The record of a text's stance on it is never evidence that it is true.

proposition.criterion: The text states that AI systems already deployed or publicly available at the time of writing increase the ability of an actor seeking to cause biological harm, relative to the resources otherwise available to that actor.

entities.name: The binding barrier is physical execution rather than information
entities.note: Candidate proposition for this pack, worded from the located texts rather than from a standard formulation. Recorded at the level of the texts' own abstracts, summaries and conclusions.

proposition.criterion: The text states that access to information is not the barrier that limits biological misuse, because what remains required is physical: acquiring materials and succeeding at hands-on laboratory work.

entities.name: Published evaluations do not establish real-world biological risk
entities.note: Candidate proposition for this pack. Texts that articulate it disagree with each other about the direction of the error.

proposition.criterion: The text states that published evaluations or benchmarks of AI systems' biological capability do not, as conducted, establish the level of real-world biological misuse risk.

entities.name: Biological design tools pose risks distinct from those of language models
entities.note: Candidate proposition for this pack.

proposition.criterion: The text states that AI tools built to design or predict biological molecules or systems create misuse risks that differ in kind, in the actors they affect or in the governance they require, from those of general-purpose language models.

entities.name: Synthesis-order screening is a control point for AI-related biological risk
entities.note: Candidate proposition for this pack. Recorded at the policy level only; no record states how screening is performed or how it could fail.

proposition.criterion: The text states that screening orders for synthesised nucleic acids is a control point on which mitigation of AI-related biological risk depends.

entities.name: Public release of model weights increases biological misuse risk
entities.note: Candidate proposition for this pack.

proposition.criterion: The text states that making model weights publicly available increases the risk of biological misuse, or that some models should for that reason not be released openly.

entities.name: Assessment must cover actors who already hold relevant skills
entities.note: Candidate proposition for this pack. It concerns the scope of assessment, not the size of any risk.

proposition.criterion: The text states that assessment of AI-related biological risk must cover actors who already hold relevant scientific skills, and not only actors without them.

openQuestions.question: The proposition codes B1 to B7 used here clash with the dataset's existing codes B1 to B6 (deceptive alignment, the treacherous turn, strategic concealment, scheming and two others). Schema validation rejects duplicate proposition codes, so the pack's codes cannot be admitted as written.
openQuestions.recommended: Keep B1–B7 inside the pack, where the brief set them, and re-letter them on admission to an unused letter — D1–D7 would be free (the dataset uses A, B, C, E, G, M and Y). The integrator should decide the letter once, for the whole pack, and record the mapping in the pack README.

openQuestions.question: Every proposition here carries an empty `terms` list, so no record holds an earliest-located-use-of-a-name role. "Uplift" is a usual name for B1 in these texts and appears in two recorded passages.
openQuestions.recommended: Register "uplift" as B1's usual name only together with an earliest-located-term record, and search for its earliest located use separately; schema validation requires exactly one such record once a term is listed. Until then leaving `terms` empty is the honest state.

openQuestions.question: Three propositions (B3, B4, B7) have no contesting text in this draft. For B3 that is because a text asserting that current evaluations do measure real-world risk was not located; for B4 and B7 no located text disputes the distinction or the scope.
openQuestions.recommended: Treat the absence as a search result, not a finding, and leave it as it is. If the maintainer wants it on the record, a bounded negative record per proposition would need its own search terms and scope, which this pass did not run.

openQuestions.question: Anthropic's post is both a developer's argument and a report of its own trials. This pass records only its methodological and argument-level statements, while the `evaluations` pass may record its result.
openQuestions.recommended: Keep the split, and have the integrator check that no evaluation result is recorded twice across the two drafts. Cite the same source key (`anthropic-biorisk`) in both so the quotation budget for that page is counted once.

openQuestions.question: Sandbrink's preprint was revised eight times between June and December 2023, and the abstract wording changed; this draft cites v1 only.
openQuestions.recommended: Keep v1 as the dated expression for the earliest-located roles. If a later version is wanted for the argument's developed form, record it as a separate document version rather than editing these records.

openQuestions.question: The RAND working paper (Brent and McKelvey) is marked by its publisher as not formally reviewed or edited, and a later RAND perspective with a similar title (PEA3853-1) was seen but not retrieved.
openQuestions.recommended: Keep the working paper as the dated expression and record the perspective separately if a later pass retrieves it; do not merge them into one document.

openQuestions.question: Proposition B2 has no articulating record after the correction of ab-arg-b2-batalis-articulates, so its earliest-located articulation role has no holder. The earliest located text on B2 is now the contesting record ab-arg-b2-soice-contests (6 June 2023).
openQuestions.recommended: Leave the role without a holder rather than promoting a text that does not meet the criterion; schema validation requires a holder only where an articulation exists, and schema 2.16's `withheld` list is for a role withheld from existing articulations. A later pass should search for an articulation of B2 — the paywalled venues listed in `howWeSearched` are the obvious gap — and record it with the role if one is found.

openQuestions.question: ab-arg-b2-batalis-articulates now holds a stance its id does not name. Ids are not yet stable (the pack is unmerged), but this one is cited in research/ai-bio/audit/audit-A.json, verification.json, audit-sample.json, pack.md and cross-family-input-2026-10-28.md.
openQuestions.recommended: Keep the id for now, so the finding and its correction stay traceable, and rename it to ab-arg-b2-batalis-bears-on at admission, when pack.json is rebuilt and the references can be updated in one step.

openQuestions.question: The audit sampled four of the records whose publication date is attested only by a source that was not cited as evidence. The same gap remains in the records it did not sample: ab-arg-b1-soice-articulates and ab-arg-b5-soice-articulates (arxiv-2306-03809-abs), ab-arg-b5-sandbrink-articulates and ab-arg-b7-sandbrink-articulates (arxiv-2306-13952-abs), ab-arg-b3-brent-articulates (arxiv-2506-13798-abs), ab-arg-b4-batalis-articulates and ab-arg-b7-batalis-bears-on (cset-biorisk-explainer), and ab-arg-b1-mouton-contests (rand-mouton-2024-page).
openQuestions.recommended: Apply the same correction to those eight records in a separately authorised pass: one evidence item per record citing the listing or landing page for the date, as the corrected records now do. The budgets allow it; each of those five sources is used for dates only and has its full allowance left. This pass changed only the records the auditors named.

openQuestions.question: ab-arg-b1-soice-articulates rests on the same sentence as ab-arg-b2-soice-contests and drops the same condition ("as soon as they are credibly identified"), and it carries the source's own category term where the B2 record substitutes a neutral paraphrase. Neither auditor sampled it.
openQuestions.recommended: Restore the condition there too, and replace the category term with the neutral paraphrase used in ab-arg-b2-soice-contests, in the same separately authorised pass. It was left unchanged here because no finding covered it.

openQuestions.question: The support role of the evidence is used against the proposition rather than against the record: every contesting record in this draft carries only `support: "contradicts"` passages, and the one bears_on record carries only `context`. The dataset uses `supports` for the passage that shows the text contesting or bearing on the proposition (all 213 `contests_proposition` and all 293 `bears_on_proposition` claims in data/claims.json), and schema validation requires at least one supporting item on a supported record (src/domain/schema.ts, "Supported and contested claims require supporting evidence"). Neither auditor raised it.
openQuestions.recommended: Before admission, relabel those passages `supports` — the support role describes the evidence's relation to the record, and the record is that the text contests or bears on the proposition — and keep `contradicts` for a passage that tells against the record itself. Seven records still have no supporting item: ab-arg-b1-mouton-contests, ab-arg-b1-peppin-contests, ab-arg-b1-itif-contests, ab-arg-b2-anthropic-contests, ab-arg-b5-moulange-contests, ab-arg-b6-kapoor-contests and ab-arg-b7-batalis-bears-on. The corrections of 2026-10-28 incidentally gave ab-arg-b2-soice-contests, ab-arg-b2-brent-contests and ab-arg-b2-batalis-articulates a supporting date item, which is not a disposition of this question. Nothing was relabelled here, since it is outside the findings this pass applied.

openQuestions.question: Should `states_evaluation_result` enter the schema as a predicate, and should its `attributes.evaluation` block (what, how, result, caveats) be added to the claim schema?
openQuestions.recommended: Yes, if any of this pack is admitted: 24 of the 49 records here use it, and no existing predicate carries a report's stated result with the report's own caveats. Keep `reports_evaluation_of` for naming an evaluation category, as the dataset already does.

openQuestions.question: `evaluation_engagement` allows `organisation` subjects and objects only (`src/domain/predicates.ts`, enforced by the schema's subject-type check), but the UK institute is typed `public_body` in the dataset (`uk-ai-security-institute`), so the two UK engagement records here — `ab-ev-gpt5-uk-aisi-engagement` and `ab-ev-claude37-uk-aisi-engagement` — cannot be admitted as structured. Auditor A raised this on the first of the two; the second has the identical defect and was not separately audited. Neither record was changed, because the pack changes neither the dataset nor the schema.
openQuestions.recommended: A maintainer decision is needed before either record is admitted. Preferred: widen the predicate's subjects to include `public_body` rather than retyping the institute, since the existing US records use `us-ai-safety-institute`, which is typed `organisation`, so the dataset is already inconsistent on this point. The alternative, if the predicate is to stay as it is, is to re-record each engagement from the document's side (subject the system card, with the institute named in the statement), which loses the engagement relation and so is worse for a reader. Whichever is chosen, `ab-ev-gpt5-uk-aisi-engagement` carries the limit in its own qualification and `ab-ev-claude37-uk-aisi-engagement` should be given the same wording when the decision is applied.

openQuestions.question: The NIST summary page for the upgraded Claude 3.5 Sonnet carries the footer 'Released November 19, 2024, Updated March 20, 2025', the same mutable-source problem auditor B found on the o1 page. The footer string was verified in the cache on 2026-10-28; no date was changed. What remains for a checker who can reach the Internet Archive is to compare the released and updated expressions of both NIST pages, which neither page describes.

openQuestions.question: Auditor A asks, for all three Biological Weapons Convention records (ab-gov-bwc-us-wp14-ai-verification, ab-gov-bwc-uk-wp27-biotech-ai-threats, ab-gov-bwc-japan-wp28-misuse-risk), whether states_provision suits a national statement at all: the predicate's description is about an exact framework edition stating one provision.
openQuestions.recommended: Decide before admission. A national statement is not an instrument's provision; the honest options are a new predicate for a position stated in a document submitted to a treaty meeting, or recording these as propositions in the arguments strand with the document as the text that articulates them. The three records now use provision kind 'risk_domain' consistently, which keeps them readable either way, and none of them says that any State Party acted.

openQuestions.question: The schema-fit defects the auditors found in the sampled records run through records they did not sample, which this task left untouched. openQuestions.question: The schema's provision kinds have no entry for an instrument's standing (whether following it is voluntary or expected practice) or for whom it addresses. The audited records now use 'exception', 'required_action' and 'threshold' as the nearest admitted kinds.

timeline.event: The United States Department of Health and Human Services, through its Office of the Secretary, published the Screening Framework Guidance for Providers of Synthetic Double-Stranded DNA in the Federal Register of 13 October 2010, stating that it sets out recommended baseline standards for the gene and genome synthesis industry and other providers regarding the screening of orders.

The Administration for Strategic Preparedness and Response published a proposed revised screening framework guidance for providers and users of synthetic oligonucleotides in the Federal Register of 29 April 2022, submitting it for public consideration and comment for a period of 60 days.

The preprint "Can large language models democratize access to dual-use biotechnology?" (arXiv v1, 6 June 2023) states that large language models will make pandemic-class agents widely accessible even to people with little or no laboratory training.

The preprint "Can large language models democratize access to dual-use biotechnology?" (arXiv v1, 6 June 2023) states that the agents it discusses would become widely accessible as soon as they are credibly identified, even to people with little or no laboratory training, against the premise that laboratory execution is the binding barrier.

The preprint of 6 June 2023 states that promising nonproliferation measures include pre-release evaluations of language models by third parties, curation of training datasets, and verifiable screening of all DNA generated by synthesis providers.

Sandbrink's preprint on AI and biological misuse (arXiv v1, 24 June 2023) states that large language models such as GPT-4 are already able to provide dual-use information that could have enabled historical biological weapons efforts to succeed.

Sandbrink's preprint (arXiv v1, 24 June 2023) differentiates large language models from biological design tools, stating that language models in particular lower barriers to biological misuse while design tools expand the capabilities of sophisticated actors.
Sandbrink's preprint (arXiv v1, 24 June 2023) states that enhanced screening of gene synthesis is among the measures key to reducing the risks it describes.

Sandbrink's preprint (arXiv v1, 24 June 2023) states that biological design tools will expand the capabilities of sophisticated actors, and proposes interventions to deter biological misuse by such actors.

H.R. 4702 of the 118th Congress, the Securing Gene Synthesis Act, was introduced in the House of Representatives on 18 July 2023 by Representative Anna G. Eshoo, referred to the Committee on Energy and Commerce, and referred to its Subcommittee on Health on 21 July 2023.

S. 2399 of the 118th Congress, the Artificial Intelligence and Biosecurity Risk Assessment Act, was introduced in the Senate on 19 July 2023 by Senator Edward J. Markey, with Senator Ted Budd as an original cosponsor, and read twice and referred to the Committee on Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions.

S. 2400 of the 118th Congress, the Securing Gene Synthesis Act, was introduced in the Senate on 19 July 2023 by Senator Edward J. Markey and read twice and referred to the Committee on Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions.

"Open-Sourcing Highly Capable Foundation Models" (arXiv v1, submitted 29 September 2023) states that for some highly capable foundation models likely to be developed in the near future, open-sourcing may pose sufficiently extreme risks to outweigh the benefits, and names access to biological weapons knowledge among the dangerous capabilities at issue.

The Administration for Strategic Preparedness and Response published the Screening Framework Guidance for Providers and Users of Synthetic Nucleic Acids in the Federal Register of 13 October 2023, stating that it sets out baseline standards for the gene and genome synthesis industry and best practices for all entities involved in the provision, use and transfer of synthetic nucleic acids.

The 2023 Screening Framework Guidance for Providers and Users of Synthetic Nucleic Acids states that advances in the field motivated the United States Government to review and revise the 2010 Screening Framework Guidance for Providers of Synthetic Double-Stranded DNA, and cites the 2010 guidance at 75 FR 62820.

The preprint "Towards Responsible Governance of Biological Design Tools" (arXiv v1, 27 November 2023) states that biological design tools pose distinct regulatory challenges and that regulatory proposals tailored to large language models may be less effective for them.

The preprint of 27 November 2023 states that the design capabilities of biological design tools could be used to evade DNA screening techniques, against the premise that screening at synthesis is a dependable control point.
The preprint of 27 November 2023 identifies, among the challenges of regulating biological design tools, the potential for safeguards to be circumvented by open-sourcing model weights.

CSET's explainer "AI and Biorisk" (December 2023) states that the barrier to scientific information is not high even for beginners, and that feasibility depends on both information and hands-on production success, without stating which of the two limits biological misuse.
CSET's explainer of December 2023 treats biological design tools as a separate class from chatbots, stating that their use in its current state requires both scientific and programming expertise.

CSET's explainer of December 2023 states that the biorisk landscape is not uniform and that specific scenarios and actors should be assessed individually, without stating that assessment must cover actors who already hold relevant skills.

RAND's red-team study states that it found no statistically significant difference in the viability of the plans produced by its red cells with or without large language model assistance, for the two models and the fifteen cells it describes.
RAND published 'The Operational Risks of AI in Large-Scale Biological Attacks: Results of a Red-Team Study' (RR-A2977-2) on 25 January 2024.

RAND's report on the operational risks of AI in large-scale biological attacks (RR-A2977-2, 25 January 2024) states that it found no statistically significant difference in the overall viability of biological weapon attack plans generated with or without the aid of the large language models it tested, and that such planning is beyond the capability frontier of the models available in summer 2023.

"On the Societal Impact of Open Foundation Models" (arXiv v1, 27 February 2024) states that across several misuse vectors, biological weapons among them, current research is insufficient to characterise the marginal risk of open foundation models relative to pre-existing technologies.

The Office of Science and Technology Policy released the Framework for Nucleic Acid Synthesis Screening on 29 April 2024, and the copy served from the Biden White House archive on 28 October 2026 is marked as revised in September 2024, with April 2024 given as version 1.

An ITIF commentary of 30 April 2024 states that experts, having studied the issue more closely, have concluded that large language models do not introduce a new set of capabilities or significantly enhance existing ones that could lead to a biological attack.

The WMDP benchmark paper states that it publicly releases a dataset of 3,668 multiple-choice questions serving as a proxy measurement of hazardous knowledge in biosecurity, cybersecurity and chemical security, developed by a consortium of academics and technical consultants and filtered to remove sensitive information before release.

The UK institute's May 2024 evaluations update states that several of the five publicly available large language models it tested demonstrated expert-level knowledge of chemistry and biology, answering over 600 private expert-written chemistry and biology questions at levels similar to humans with PhD-level training.

The UK institute, then named the AI Safety Institute, published 'Advanced AI evaluations at AISI: May update' on 20 May 2024, stating that it had tested leading AI models for cyber, chemical, biological and agent capabilities and for safeguard effectiveness.

The UK screening guidance on synthetic nucleic acids for users and providers was published on GOV.UK on 8 October 2024, described there as guidance for users and providers involved in the provision, use and transfer of synthetic nucleic acids and of benchtop equipment that synthesises nucleic acids in the UK.

The White House issued the national security memorandum on advancing United States leadership in artificial intelligence, harnessing AI for national security objectives and fostering AI safety, security and trustworthiness, posted on its briefing-room page under the date 24 October 2024.

NIST states that US AISI and UK AISI conducted a joint pre-deployment evaluation of Anthropic's upgraded Claude 3.5 Sonnet, with biological capabilities among the four domains tested, and that the findings were shared with Anthropic before public release.

The joint pre-deployment evaluation summary for Anthropic's upgraded Claude 3.5 Sonnet states that US AISI evaluated the model on a set of multiple-choice biology research task questions and that its performance was comparable to the reference models and significantly below measured human expert baselines in most instances.

The joint pre-deployment evaluation summary for the upgraded Claude 3.5 Sonnet states that US AISI piloted an evaluation method that augments the model with access to bioinformatic tools, and that when tested with Sonnet 3.5 this resulted in increased performance beyond the model alone, at times exceeding measured human expert baselines.

The Llama 3 paper states that its uplift testing for chemical and biological weapons found no significant uplift in performance related to use of the Llama 3 model, both in an aggregate comparison with a web-only control condition and in its subgroup breakdowns.
The Llama 3 authors at Meta published 'The Llama 3 Herd of Models' as arXiv:2407.21783, first submitted on 31 July 2024, with the version read here submitted on 23 November 2024.

The Llama 3 paper states that, after validating its uplift results with CBRNE subject matter experts, it assesses that there is a low risk that release of the Llama 3 models will increase ecosystem risk related to biological or chemical weapon attacks.

The preprint "The Reality of AI and Biorisk" (arXiv v1, 2 December 2024) states that the available literature does not support the notion that access to biological information and planning through current, publicly available large language models can significantly increase biorisk.

The preprint "The Reality of AI and Biorisk" (arXiv v1, 2 December 2024) states that existing studies of AI-related biorisk are nascent, often speculative, or limited in methodological maturity and transparency.

The o1 System Card states that its evaluations found o1 can help experts with the operational planning of reproducing a known biological threat, which it says meets OpenAI's medium risk threshold, and that the Safety Advisory Group classified the pre-mitigation model as medium risk for CBRN.

The o1 System Card states that OpenAI's Preparedness evaluations cover four risk categories, one of which is CBRN (chemical, biological, radiological, nuclear), and that o1 was evaluated in accordance with the Preparedness Framework.
The o1 System Card states that the models do not enable non-experts to create biological threats, because creating such a threat requires hands-on laboratory skills that the models cannot replace.

The joint pre-deployment evaluation summary for OpenAI's o1 states that US AISI found the model's performance on a set of multiple-choice biology research task questions to be generally comparable to the best-performing reference models tested across an array of question sets.

NIST states that US AISI and UK AISI conducted a joint pre-deployment evaluation of OpenAI's o1 across three domains including biological capabilities, and OpenAI's own system card states that pre-deployment evaluations by the two institutes were conducted on a version of o1 and are not included in the card.

The Virology Capabilities Test paper states that it presents a large language model benchmark measuring the capability to troubleshoot complex virology laboratory protocols, built from the inputs of dozens of expert virologists.

The Virology Capabilities Test paper states that expert virologists with internet access scored an average of 22.1% on the benchmark's questions within their own sub-areas of expertise, while the most performant model it tested, OpenAI's o3, reached 43.8% accuracy and outperformed 94% of those experts within their sub-areas.
Executive Order 14292, Improving the Safety and Security of Biological Research, is dated 5 May 2025 in the Federal Register print of the order.

Anthropic's ASL-3 activation post states that it had not yet determined whether Claude Opus 4 definitively passed the capabilities threshold requiring ASL-3 protections, that continued improvements in CBRN-related knowledge and capabilities meant clearly ruling out ASL-3 risks was not possible as it had been for every previous model, and that it deployed the model with ASL-3 measures as a precautionary and provisional action.

Anthropic published 'Activating AI Safety Level 3 protections' on 22 May 2025, stating that it had activated the ASL-3 Deployment and Security Standards of its Responsible Scaling Policy in conjunction with launching Claude Opus 4.

Anthropic's ASL-3 activation post states that experiments showed access to Claude Sonnet 3.7 helped participants do somewhat better on tasks related to CBRN weapon acquisition than those with standard internet access, and that all participants' plans still had critical failures.

The RAND working paper "Contemporary AI foundation models increase biological weapons risk" (WR-A3853-1, arXiv v1 of 12 June 2025) states that contemporary AI models can meaningfully contribute to biological weapons development, against published safety assessments that assert minimal risk.

The RAND working paper of 12 June 2025 states that safety assessments mistakenly assume that biological weapons development requires tacit knowledge, that is, expertise gained through experience that cannot be conveyed in words.

The RAND working paper of 12 June 2025 states that flawed safety assessments resting on tacit knowledge and inadequate benchmarks may create a false sense of security, leading to weak safeguards and regulatory gaps.

The RAND working paper of 12 June 2025 states that safety assessments rely on benchmarks that overlook the full range of potential threat actors and fail to account for how AI could enhance the capabilities of skilled individuals as well as enabling non-experts.

The ChatGPT Agent System Card states that OpenAI conducted human red teaming on biological risk as one of two key risk areas, and sets out an overview table of its biological and chemical evaluations.
OpenAI published the ChatGPT Agent System Card, dated 17 July 2025 on its cover.

The ChatGPT Agent System Card states that OpenAI invited seven experts with biosafety and biosecurity backgrounds to spend three to five hours with a helpful-only version of the model and to score it in a survey, and that experts noted an average success rate of about 7.7 on a scale of 1 to 10 on the tasks they attempted.

The ChatGPT Agent System Card states that OpenAI decided to treat the launch as High capability in the Biological and Chemical domain under its Preparedness Framework, activating the associated safeguards, while stating that it does not have definitive evidence that the model could meaningfully help a novice to create severe biological harm and has taken a precautionary approach.

OpenAI's ChatGPT Agent System Card reports that two SecureBio virologists carried out about ten hours of manual red-teaming with ChatGPT agent, and that SecureBio also supplied an external assessment within the card's biological evaluations.

OpenAI's GPT-5 System Card states that it gave the US Center for AI Standards and Innovation early access to gpt-5-thinking under a newly signed, updated agreement, and that CAISI evaluated the model's biological and chemical capabilities and its safeguards.
OpenAI published the GPT-5 System Card, dated 13 August 2025 on its cover.

The GPT-5 System Card states that OpenAI decided to treat gpt-5-thinking as High capability in the Biological and Chemical domain under its Preparedness Framework, activating the associated safeguards, while stating that it does not have definitive evidence that the model could meaningfully help a novice to create severe biological harm.

OpenAI's GPT-5 System Card states that the UK AI Security Institute evaluated gpt-5-thinking's biological and chemical capabilities and its safeguards, with access to prototype safeguards and non-public information sources as part of a longer-term collaboration.

The GPT-5 System Card states that the UK AI Security Institute's safeguards team identified multiple model-level jailbreaks that overcome gpt-5-thinking's built-in refusal logic without degrading model capabilities, and that one of them evades all layers of mitigations and is being patched.

The Grok 4 Model Card states that the area of highest concern is the model's expert-level biology capabilities, which significantly exceed human expert baselines on the benchmarks used, while stating that these evaluations measure dual-use knowledge and that a high score indicates greater capability to enable weapons development, not necessarily increased risk.
xAI published the Grok 4 Model Card, the expression read stating that it was last updated on 20 August 2025.

Anthropic's Frontier Red Team post "LLMs and biorisk" (5 September 2025) states that its 2024 pilot study, while not providing strong evidence either way about AI uplift, suggested that tacit knowledge may not be as significant a bottleneck as many have suggested.

Anthropic's Frontier Red Team post of 5 September 2025 states that text-based uplift trials of the kind it reports are imperfect proxies for real-world scenarios, which involve further factors it names.

The Claude Sonnet 4.5 system card states that the model demonstrated enhanced performance on several biological risk evaluations while remaining below ASL-4 rule-out thresholds, and that Anthropic has not determined whether it passed the ASL-3 capabilities threshold but cannot clearly rule out ASL-3 risks, so deploys it with ASL-3 measures as a precautionary, provisional action.

The Claude Sonnet 4.5 system card states that its CBRN evaluations primarily focus on biological risks with the largest consequences and sets out separate ASL-3 and ASL-4 threat models for that domain.
Anthropic published the Claude Sonnet 4.5 system card, dated September 2025 on its cover.
Google DeepMind published the Gemini 3 Pro model card, the expression read stating that it was last updated in May 2026.

The Gemini 3 Pro model card states that the model was evaluated as set out in Google DeepMind's Frontier Safety Framework of September 2025 and did not reach any critical capability level, and that in the CBRN domain the uplift level 1 critical capability level was not reached.

The International Gene Synthesis Consortium published version 3.1 of its Harmonized Screening Protocol, dated 1 June 2026, which states that it sets out the standards and practices that the consortium's provider and manufacturer members apply to prevent the misuse of synthetic nucleic acids.
